Get started with polyviz

polyviz.Rmd

polyviz draws interactive D3 charts from plain R data frames — no JavaScript, no grammar to learn, one function call per chart. This is the five-minute tour: a first chart, a second, the automatic behaviours and how to override them, layers, theming, and the way out to a printed page. The charts open in your Viewer as you go, so paste along; none of the chunks run while the vignette builds.

Install 

# install.packages("devtools")
devtools::install_github("jastephan63/polyviz")

Everything the charts need ships in the package, bundled D3 included. Python is optional (profiling falls back to pure R without it), and headless Chrome is only needed at the very end, for pv_save().

A first chart, in one line

Fourteen real Swiss open-government datasets are bundled. pv_weather holds six years of daily weather in Lucerne, from MeteoSwiss — hand it straight to a line chart:

library(polyviz)

pv_line(pv_weather, x = "date", y = "temp_mean")

The chart draws itself in, follows your light/dark setting, re-renders when its container resizes, and a crosshair tooltip reads out the exact value under the cursor. That is the whole interface: a data frame, column names, options.

Add a title and a source line

Every chart shares the same heading options — title, subtitle, and a small grey source credit at the bottom left, newsroom style:

pv_line(pv_weather, x = "date", y = "temp_mean",
        title = "Six years of Lucerne weather",
        subtitle = "Daily mean temperature",
        source = "Source: MeteoSwiss")

A second chart type

All 36 chart types work the same way. Bars want one row per bar, so aggregate first — and invalid data fails with a clear R-side message rather than a broken chart:

sales <- aggregate(revenue ~ region, pv_sales, sum)
pv_bar(sales, x = "region", y = "revenue", title = "Revenue by region")

The “auto” defaults, and overriding them

Charts adapt to their data and their pixels at render time. Here fifteen municipality names are too long to sit side by side under vertical bars, so horizontal = "auto" — the default — flips the chart sideways: labels upright down the left, the exact value at each bar’s end:

f25 <- subset(pv_fiscal, year == 2025)
top15 <- head(f25[order(-f25$equalization_chf), ], 15)

pv_bar(top15, x = "municipality", y = "equalization_chf",
       title = "Largest equalization payments, 2025",
       source = "Source: LUSTAT Statistik Luzern")

Every automatic behaviour has an explicit TRUE/FALSE/"auto" override. Force the vertical layout back and you can see what the default saved you from — fifteen labels fighting for the same row:

pv_bar(top15, x = "municipality", y = "equalization_chf",
       horizontal = FALSE)

Layer with the pipe

Modifiers pipe onto an existing chart. pv_trend() fits a smoother with a confidence ribbon:

pv_scatter(f25, x = "resource_index", y = "equalization_chf") |>
  pv_trend("loess")

The same shape gives you small multiples (pv_facet()), annotations (pv_annotate()), print-safe hatching (pv_textures()), and linked selection across charts (pv_link()).

Theme and locale, in two lines 

pv_set_theme(pv_theme_paper())  # print-first: white surface, luminance-ordered colours
pv_locale("de-CH")              # Swiss numbers (10'000) and German month names

Every chart built from here on wears both. pv_set_theme() also takes your own brand colours — with an accessibility check on the way in — and pv_reset_theme() and pv_locale(NULL) restore the defaults.

Into a paper

pv_save() picks the format from the file extension — a crisp 2x PNG for Word and slides, true vector PDF for LaTeX, standalone SVG, or one self-contained interactive HTML file:

w <- pv_bar(sales, x = "region", y = "revenue",
            title = "Revenue by region")
pv_save(w, "revenue.png")
pv_save(w, "revenue.pdf")

The capture formats render the chart for real in headless Chrome (the chromote package plus a Chrome-based browser). Knitting to Word or PDF needs no call at all — a chart in a chunk becomes a print-quality figure by itself. Sizing, alt text, animated GIFs, and whole PowerPoint decks: vignette("embedding-charts").

Where to go next 

pv_suggest(pv_weather)  # which charts fit this data frame?
pv_demo()               # every chart family, live, with controls
  • The live gallery — all 36 chart types, interactive, each explained and running on real Swiss open data, with the R code that made it.
  • pv_demo() opens the same idea as a Shiny app on your machine, with live controls for each chart’s main options.
  • pv_suggest() inspects a data frame and prints runnable chart calls with the real column names filled in, each with a line of reasoning — every suggestion is proven to run before it is offered.
  • The cheatsheet (PDF) fits the whole package on a desk-side sheet.
  • The reference site documents every function; the other vignettes go deeper — exploring a dataset (vignette("polyviz-eda")), charts in papers (vignette("embedding-charts")), live Swiss open data (vignette("swiss-open-data")), and the SQL/SAS/Python backends (vignette("polyglot-backend")).
